What does the research actually show?

A curated database of peer-reviewed studies, policy reports, and investigative journalism on AI, automation, and labor markets.

From recent research

Which numbers can you actually cite?

Every fact below is a short, number-bearing statement quoted verbatim from a source in the research database. Each is rated on two independent scales: how politically noteworthy it is for progressive advocacy (inequality, corporate power, environment, worker power) and how truthful its underlying evidence is. A fact can score high on one and low on the other; the point is to know which is which before you use it.

Pilot release. Ratings are editorial judgments made against a written rubric and reviewed by hand; the “take note” line under each fact is the defensible phrasing. Click through to the tracker entry or the source before publishing a number.

No facts match the current filters.
01 North Star

We want an AI that people have a say over, that widens who gets to know and do things, and whose returns reach the people whose knowledge built it.

Whether AI is good for the people who work alongside it is not a property of the technology. The same model can draft the tedious first version of a document and hand a worker back an hour of judgment, or it can time their breaks, score their calls, set their pace, and strip out the discretion that made the job theirs. Which one happens turns on who decides how the thing gets deployed, and today that is almost never the people doing the work. We want workers at that table before the decision is made, with the standing to say no. What we are fighting is the version of this technology that shows up as a surveillance and speed‑up device with a chat window on the front.

Away from work the stakes split the same way. AI can put expertise within reach of people who could never afford it, and open doors that a credential or a zip code used to close. It can also be pointed at sorting people: who gets the apartment, the loan, the shift, the interview, the benefit, decided with all the bias of the record the model learned from, landing first and hardest on communities of color. Then there is the money. These systems are built out of what all of us wrote, drew, measured, and worked out, so the gains belong to all of us in a way the present arrangement does not reflect. A society that gets richer this way should feel richer: more security, more time, better public goods. The alternative is already taking shape, with the returns pooling in a few firms while everyone else pays the freight in utility bills, water and land, public subsidy, and work that pays less and holds together worse.

02 Legitimize

Worth doing either way

Most of what follows does not depend on AI being world‑historical. These are policies we would want if the technology stalls out at merely useful, and the ones we will need most if it does not. If AI is going to run through work and public life, and it looks like it will, this is the floor. The descriptions are first drafts and will get sharper.

  1. A worker voice in deployment Before a system goes in, the people it will be used on should have a say in what it monitors, what it automates, and what happens to the jobs it changes. That is broader than most of what is on the table in Washington or inside the labs, which is largely about how models get built rather than how they get used on people. It should be broader.
  2. Pre‑clearance before release Systems capable of serious harm should have to clear a bar before deployment rather than be recalled after the damage. That review is also where algorithmic discrimination gets caught: testing for disparate outcomes belongs in the condition of approval, not in a voluntary report published a year later.
  3. Public options in AI Broadly defined, and we are not precious about the form: public compute and public research, a government model, open‑weight models kept genuinely open, procurement that keeps an alternative alive. What matters is that basic capability is not something you can only rent from three companies.
  4. Universal health care In the United States, health insurance rides on a job, which makes losing that job to a machine a medical event as well as a financial one. Nothing else here does as much to make a churning labor market survivable, and it is the clearest case of an old fight that AI makes newly urgent.
  5. Unemployment insurance and retraining that work UI reaches too few workers, replaces too little of a paycheck, and runs out too soon. Retraining money is small and badly aimed. Fix both and you help everyone who loses a job, including the many who will never be told that AI is why.
  6. Cash through the transition A universal, fully refundable Child Tax Credit is where we would start. Cash covers the cases no categorical program anticipated, and in a transition nobody can forecast, that is most of the cases.
  7. Pay for it with corporate taxes The AI firms are the obvious place to start and too narrow a base to stop at. The gains show up across the corporate sector, at every firm that buys capability it did not have to build. Tax the returns where they land.
03 Provoke

Worth building toward

These are exploratory. We are not putting them forward as this session’s bills, and the design details are unsettled. Each carries the germ of something, though: an answer to what a society does with wealth on the scale AI’s advocates keep promising. If they are right, the interesting question is not how to cushion the fall. It is what to buy with the surplus.

  1. A four‑day week If output per hour rises the way the forecasts say, part of the gain should come back as time instead of all of it as output. Same pay, four days, on the logic that produced the weekend and the eight‑hour day. Earlier productivity booms were partly cashed out in hours. The last few were not.
  2. A guaranteed income If the models are built from everyone’s knowledge, everyone holds a claim on what they earn. A guaranteed income is the most direct way to pay that claim and the least paternalistic. It also does what no jobs program can, which is reach people whose work was never paid in the first place.
  3. A jobs corps funded by the surplus There is work that badly needs doing and that no market will pay for: cleaning contaminated land and water, repairing what a warming climate is taking apart, caring for children and elders at the scale families actually need. A public jobs corps, funded out of how much richer this technology makes us, could hire straight into it.

Where this goes next. A first pass, published early on purpose. Each item here will be built out with the precedents, bills and research behind it, the way the entries in the Policy Map already are, and the exploratory set will be argued with before any of it is proposed.

Welcome to our AI dashboard.

The AI transition is one of the most challenging transformations of our times. We don’t know what this technology will become, how the economy will absorb it, or what policy should do in response.

  1. Research. It’s unclear how the technology itself will take shape. Will it be a normal technology, as Arvind Narayanan and Sayash Kapoor argue, or is it more like electricity, where the whole economy eventually reorganizes around it?
  2. Economy. Even as the technology evolves, how the economy absorbs it is a separate question. Will AI’s effect on the labor market be sudden and large, or slower and more jagged as it works its way into existing firms and institutions?
  3. Policy. And even then, it’s hard to know how to react. What policies safeguard against the downsides, amplify what’s good, and make sure this broadly helps people? Should we work through the policies we already have, or does a genuinely new era demand bigger and different ideas? How much can we steer the technology, and how much should we just plan on absorbing its effects?

Each question calls for a different kind of answer, which is how this dashboard is organized. We’re learning here alongside everyone else, but we think what we’ve built can contribute to a better AI transition.

Research

Our research tracker is a searchable, tagged list of work on AI and its impact, broadly defined. Alongside it is our fact bank, meant as a resource for the community as a whole: specific sentences you can consider using, each with a caveat section laying out what the finding actually supports and where it has been stretched.

How this section is built. To cover this much ground, the tracker and fact bank are summarized with the help of AI and then human review. We’ve built skills to check the output for accuracy, but as with any secondhand source, verify anything you plan to cite or build on. Terminal-based AI tools are becoming more important for ideas-based work, and we’d rather experiment with putting them into our own workflow than only write about them.

Economy

The first section is a real-time data tracker that pulls monthly and quarterly values from the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA), and other government sources. Rather than waiting on long-term forecasts, it provides immediate, accessible feedback on the exact macroeconomic metrics we are watching as the technology rolls out.

The second section tracks how AI is showing up in the labor market. Rather than running complicated statistical tests, we tell a story about the different ways you might look at this, to give a broader sense of what is and isn’t moving. We update it with each new data release, and we show the range of tools economists are bringing to the question.

There will be no jobs day where AI’s effect on the labor market becomes undeniable and forces a policy response. In that way it’s less like 9/11 or the COVID lockdowns and more like climate change: the impact accumulates without ever announcing itself. We hope this makes it easier to follow while we’re still early.

Policy

Our policy map includes nearly every idea people have raised for making AI safe and broadly beneficial. Click through any of them and you’ll find the major bills and initiatives from that policy’s advocates. If you’re trying to compile what has actually been introduced, start here.

This is also where we build on our theory of provoking and legitimizing policy solutions. In a world where AI is fundamentally disruptive, the work is provocation: ideas that go well beyond shoring up what we already have. In a world where AI mostly accelerates the prosperity and the inequality of the last several decades, the work is legitimation, and that’s the harder job. We already know what those solutions look like. They have been contested for thirty years.

Created and maintained by members of the Ideas Team: Becky Chao, Mike Konczal, and Christelle Prophete.

What the data said this month.

Five sources, read on release day. Short, current, and regenerated from the same pipeline that produces everything else on this site. This is the monitoring view; the longer arguments that use these series live under Job Displacement.

Jobs

Is the labour market loosening?

The headline unemployment rate, what it looks like against the rate the CBO thinks is sustainable, and whether prime-age workers are still attached to the labour force.

Prime-age participation and employment
Ages 25–54, monthly, seasonally adjusted

Prime-age attachment is the number to watch, and it has not broken. Participation is above where it was in February 2020; the employment rate is a touch below. Neither is what a labour market absorbing a displacement shock looks like.

Payroll employment by AI-adoption group
January 2019 = 100, seasonally adjusted

Splitting payrolls by how much AI an industry reports using is the crudest version of the displacement test, and it is worth being clear that it identifies nothing. Industries that adopted AI early differ from industries that did not in size, geography, education mix and exposure to the post-2021 tech correction. The Job Displacement tab takes the question up properly, including how large an effect a design like this could actually detect.

JOLTS

Are firms still hiring?

Displacement, if it is happening, shows up in flows before it shows up in the unemployment rate. A firm that stops backfilling roles never lays anyone off. These are the four flows, split by how much AI the industry reports using.

Quits rate
Share of employment, monthly
Hires rate
Share of employment, monthly
Layoffs and discharges rate
Share of employment, monthly
Job openings rate
Share of employment plus openings, monthly

Hiring has cooled across the board, and it cooled in low-adoption industries too. Read the gap between the lines, not the level of any one of them, and read it as description rather than as an effect.

What these series are, and are not

This is the adoption split, not the national print. The published contract carries JOLTS rates grouped into thirds by industry AI adoption, because that is what the displacement analysis needs. The national headline rates that lead the JOLTS release are a separate, unbuilt step; until it exists this tab does not show them.

Rates, not levels. Every series is a share of employment, so groups of very different size are comparable. Openings are a share of employment plus openings, which is the JOLTS convention and slightly different from the others.

The grouping is fixed, the outcome moves. Industries are assigned to a group once, using adoption measured before the November 2025 BTOS question change, so the split does not shift underneath the series.

GDP

Is growth fast enough to hold unemployment down?

Okun's law gives a growth rate that keeps unemployment flat. Below it, unemployment tends to rise. It is a regularity rather than a law, and it is the cheapest way to ask whether the labour market has a growth problem or something else.

Real GDP growth
Annualised quarterly rate, 2015 onward

Growth running under breakeven with unemployment not rising is the interesting configuration, and it is roughly where we are. That combination is what a productivity story would look like, and it is also what measurement noise looks like. The Okun residual is small either way.

The fit is estimated over the full postwar sample with the two pandemic quarters excluded, because leaving them in lets 2020 set the slope for eighty years of data. The R² is what it always is for Okun's law: high enough to be useful, low enough that you should not read a single quarter's residual as news.

Productivity

Is AI showing up in output per hour?

The question that decides whether any of this is a growth story or a distribution story. It is also the series most likely to be over-read from a single quarter.

Not built yet

This tab has no data behind it, so it shows none.

When it is built it will carry BLS Major Sector Productivity: output per hour in the nonfarm business sector, quarterly and annualised, alongside unit labour costs. Neither series is in this repository yet, and no part of the pipeline fetches them.

Adding it means one new contract, following the pattern every other number here already uses: a fetch step, an exhibit that writes the card, and a publish step that emits data/tracker-productivity-data.js. The steps are written out in next_phases.md.

Who is actually adopting AI, what are they using it for, and is anyone losing a job over it?

Most of the AI-and-work debate runs on forecasts. The Census Business Trends and Outlook Survey asks roughly a million businesses, every two weeks, what they are actually doing. The answer is a chain: firms are adopting, exposure predicts which ones, the work is language work — and the last link, from adoption to job loss, is the one that does not hold.

The aggregate

How many firms are we talking about?

Census asks the same question every two weeks. In November 2025 the wording changed, so the series is drawn as two segments and never spliced.

Share of U.S. businesses using AI, and expecting to
Census Business Trends and Outlook Survey, biweekly, firm-weighted

About one firm in five, rising steadily — and four in five still report no AI use at all. Both readings are true, and the gap between them is most of the argument about what this technology is doing to work.

Adoption is rising fast in proportional terms: from under four percent to over twenty in under three years, on a base of roughly a million surveyed businesses. The level is still low. Anyone who tells you the number is dramatic and anyone who tells you it is trivial is reading the same chart.

The break matters for how you quote it. In November 2025 the question moved from AI use “in producing goods or services” to AI use “in any business function,” and the level jumped with it. The rewording also coincided with a six-week collection gap during the funding lapse, which is left open rather than interpolated. The two solid segments answer different questions and must not be joined into one series.

The dashed line is the share of firms that expect to be using AI six months out. It runs above the solid line almost everywhere, which is the ordinary pattern for stated intentions in survey data and a reason to treat forward-looking AI numbers — including forward-looking claims about headcount — as an upper bound rather than a forecast.

Exposure

Does the theory predict the practice?

Occupational exposure scores were predictions about a world that had not happened yet. Plotted against what firms report actually doing, industry by industry.

BTOS adoption against employment-weighted occupational exposure
48 three-digit NAICS industries · adoption is the pre-break mean, Sep 2023 – Nov 2025 · exposure is the PCA composite, z-scored
Each point is an industry. The fitted line is ordinary least squares on the points shown. Hover for the industry code, its exposure in standard deviations, and its adoption rate. Points labeled where the industry is recognizable: 518 data processing and hosting, 541 professional and technical services, 511 publishing, 722 food service, 484 trucking.

Yes. Industries whose workers hold more exposed occupations adopt AI substantially more, and the relationship holds under every exposure measure in the literature. The exposure research is measuring something firms act on.

The design is Tucker's, not ours

This chart and the method behind it come from Tucker (2025), who first regressed BTOS industry adoption on occupational AI exposure and reported roughly 6.7 percentage points of adoption per standard deviation of exposure, with an R² of about 0.47 at the subsector level, using crosswalked Eloundou GPT-4 exposure. What follows is a replication of that design on different inputs, not an independent discovery — and the value of running it again is that it tests how much the answer depends on which exposure measure you feed it.

Our version substitutes the Budget Lab at Yale's replication of the exposure literature and repeats the regression across all seven of its measures. Each occupation's score is collapsed to a 3-digit industry using CPS occupation-by-industry employment weights, so an industry counts as exposed to the extent that the people working in it hold exposed jobs. That industry exposure is then matched to the industry's average BTOS adoption rate over the consistent pre-rewording span.

The gradient lands close to where Tucker put it: 6.7 points per standard deviation there, inside the confidence interval here. Different exposure inputs, a different adoption window, roughly the same slope — which is the useful result, because it means the finding is not an artifact of one team's choice of exposure score.

Robustness across exposure measures

The composite is a weighted average of the underlying scores, and it is worth knowing whether the result depends on which one you pick. It does not. Every metric in the literature, including Microsoft's realized-usage measure built from a completely different kind of data, produces a positive and statistically significant slope.

Slope in percentage points of adoption per standard deviation of exposure, HC3 robust standard errors, n = 48 industries throughout. Stars: *** p<0.01, ** p<0.05, * p<0.1. The composite is the PCA-variance-weighted average of the others after z-scoring; Webb's patent-based measure is excluded because its PCA weight is an order of magnitude smaller.
Who

Which firms?

The national average hides almost everything interesting. Size is the gradient that never breaks.

Adoption by employment size class, over time
Firm-weighted within each size class, segmented at the rewording

Large firms, in information, professional services and education. Industry has the wider spread; firm size is the more consistent gradient, and the one with the biggest interpretive consequence — because adopters are large employers, the share of workers at an AI-using firm runs well ahead of the firm-weighted headline.

Big employers adopt more than small ones in every period, on both sides of the wording change, and in the separate AI supplement. BTOS weights by firm, and most firms are small. Because adopters are disproportionately large employers, the share of workers at an AI-using employer runs well above the share of firms using AI. Census publishes no employment-weighted headline, so we show the gradient rather than assert a number.

The size gradient in the AI supplement
Current AI use by employment size class, ordered smallest to largest
Industry: the spread is the story

Sector-level adoption ranges over a factor of several from top to bottom. These are the same industry cells that carry the exposure regression — the ranking below is that scatter sorted, without the exposure axis.

Current AI use by sector
Two-digit NAICS, AI supplement, firm-weighted
Most-adopting subsectors, current use and six-month expectation
Three-digit NAICS, latest collection period
Diffusion speed: who is moving fastest

Level and change are different questions. A sector can be high and static, or low and accelerating, and only the second tells you where the next few points of adoption will come from.

Change in adoption over the past six months
Percentage-point change by sector, new-wording period
What for

What is AI actually doing inside these firms?

The question the aggregate adoption rate cannot answer, and the one that determines whether adoption should displace anyone.

Which business functions use AI
Share of all businesses, multiple responses allowed, AI supplement

Language work at the commercial edge of the firm: drafting, summarizing, searching, marketing. These are tasks, and mostly tasks that sit inside jobs rather than constituting them. And the main thing holding back the non-adopters is perceived relevance, not cost, regulation or workers refusing.

AI is entering through the commercial front of the business — marketing, strategy, IT — not through production or logistics. That is close to the opposite of the pattern industrial robots followed, and it points the labor-market effect at white-collar task content rather than at manufacturing headcount.

What generative AI is used for
Among firms whose employees use generative AI, multiple responses allowed

Writing and editing dominates, then search and summarization. A displacement story has to explain how a firm gets from “our staff draft emails faster” to “we need fewer staff,” and the survey does not show that step happening yet.

Why the other four in five say no

The barriers question is the most underrated series in the supplement, because it tells you what would have to change for diffusion to continue.

Reasons firms give for not planning to use AI
Among firms not planning to adopt within six months, multiple responses allowed

Not cost. Not regulation. Not workers refusing. Overwhelmingly relevance — firms say AI does not apply to what they do — followed by not knowing how to use it. Both are ceilings that fall as capabilities broaden and knowledge spreads, which is one reason to expect diffusion to keep going rather than to plateau here.

Where

Where are the adopters?

Firm-weighted AI use by state, with the 25 largest metro areas on top. Darker is more.

AI use by state and metro area
Latest collection period, firm-weighted, share of businesses reporting AI use

Adoption is highest in the Northeast corridor, the Mountain West and Florida, and lowest across the Plains and the Deep South. The metro layer tracks the states it sits in more than it stands apart from them.

The state range runs from the high twenties down to about eleven percent, so the spread is real but narrow next to the size and industry gradients — a factor of roughly two-and-a-half across states, against a factor of several across sectors. Much of what does vary looks like industry composition: places with more information and professional-services firms sit higher.

Hover any state or metro for its estimate and standard error. These are state-level subsamples of a firm survey, so individual estimates carry meaningful sampling error — treat the broad pattern as more reliable than any single state's rank. Alaska and Rhode Island are suppressed by Census. Ten small states plus DC are unreadable at this scale, and Puerto Rico has an estimate but no polygon in the projection, so all of them appear as labelled squares below the map.

And the jobs

Do adopters say it cost anyone a job?

The supplement asks firms using AI what it did to their total employment — the closest thing to a direct measure of AI-attributed job loss in official U.S. statistics.

Self-reported effect of AI on total employment
Among businesses using AI, firm-weighted

Essentially no — and this is the link that does not hold. The overwhelming majority of AI-using firms report no employment change at all, and slightly more report an increase than a decrease. But the question cannot see forgone hiring, which is exactly where the displacement literature says to look. Read it as a bound on attributed layoffs, not a verdict on displacement.

Take the caveats seriously, because they are load-bearing. Firms have every reason not to attribute a layoff to AI, and often no clean way to know. More importantly, the question asks about employment, and the mechanism most of the microdata literature actually finds is not firing — it is not hiring. A firm that quietly stops backfilling entry-level roles reports no decrease here, and its payroll count drifts down through ordinary attrition without a single layoff.

It is also worth sitting with the sign. Slightly more adopters say AI raised their headcount than say it cut it. That is not evidence AI creates jobs — the numbers are small and self-reported either way — but it is inconsistent with the version of the story in which adoption and layoffs move together, and it is what you would expect if AI is currently making existing workers more productive at tasks they already do.

That is the shape of the evidence as it stands: a genuine, accelerating, exposure-predicted diffusion of AI into firms, doing language tasks at the commercial edge of the business, with no visible layoff signature attached to it. If displacement is happening, it is happening through the hiring door.

Which is a claim about flows, not stocks, and it needs BLS data rather than survey self-reports to test. The Job Displacement tab takes it up: whether higher-adoption industries are hiring less, whether they are laying off more, and how large an effect this design could actually detect if it were there.
What this data can and cannot tell you

Everything here is firm-weighted. BTOS weights to the population of businesses, not workers. Since adoption rises steeply with firm size, every level on this page understates worker exposure. Census publishes no employment-weighted figure and we do not construct one; the size gradient under Who is the honest substitute.

The November 2025 rewording is a real break. The question moved from AI use in producing goods or services to AI use in any business function, and the level moved with it. The two segments are never spliced, and the six-week shutdown gap is left open rather than interpolated. A handful of later periods re-ask the retired wording; those rows are kept in the tidy data and excluded from every chart, because they belong to neither series.

Suppressed cells are shown, not dropped. Census suppresses small cells; those bars appear at reduced opacity and marked with a dagger so that a thin industry is visibly thin rather than silently missing. On the map, states with no estimate are drawn in a flat neutral tone and listed in the legend.

Percentages are rounded. Values of ten percent and above are shown as whole numbers; below ten they keep one decimal, because at that end rounding would erase real differences — the gap between the share of adopters reporting an employment increase and the share reporting a decrease is the case that matters.

Geography is measured imprecisely. State and metro figures are subsamples of a firm survey and carry standard errors of a few percentage points, which is large relative to the spread across states. The map shows the levels as published; it does not test whether any two places differ.

The exposure join is the least standard thing on this page. The design is Tucker's (2025). Occupation scores come from the Budget Lab at Yale's replication of the exposure literature, aggregated to industry with CPS 2021–22 occupation-by-industry employment weights. About ten percent of employment cannot be mapped, mostly construction, which CPS codes as a single industry, and public administration. Using 2023–24 weights instead correlates at 0.99, so the choice of weight window does not drive the result.

Adoption is not causation. Nothing on this page identifies an effect of AI on anything. Industries that adopt AI differ from industries that do not in many ways, and the exposure gradient is a correlation between two industry characteristics.

Is AI displacing workers yet?

The headline unemployment rate says one thing. Look closer and it says something more specific. Five questions, asked of the labor-market data as it is released.

The short version

01 The level

Unemployment is , at or below CBO’s natural rate, and its path tracks growth about as Okun’s law predicts.

Is unemployment higher than growth alone would predict, and is a low rate hiding people who have stopped looking?

Okun’s law: GDP growth vs. change in unemployment

Okun’s law ties the change in unemployment to how fast the economy grows: strong GDP growth pulls unemployment down, weak growth pushes it up. If unemployment were rising faster than growth predicts, that would point to something structural — a displacement effect layered on the ordinary business cycle. Each point is a quarter; the line is the historical relationship, and the last four quarters are traced in sequence.

They sit close to it. Unemployment can also mislead if people stop looking for work, since they leave the labor force and the rate falls even as the market weakens. The companion check is prime-age participation, which strips out retirement.

Prime-age (25–54) labor force participation & employment rate
Monthly, seasonally adjusted, since 2000

What this cannot establish

This is the coarsest measure on the page and the last place displacement would appear. The Okun relationship leaves most quarter-to-quarter variation unexplained, so only a very large shock would clear the noise, and it is fitted on eighty years in which nothing resembling AI displacement occurs. An effect concentrated in one cohort or one sector — which is what the next two sections report — would leave no trace here at all. Read this as ruling out a macroeconomic event, not as evidence of calm.

How this is measured
Data
Real GDP and the unemployment rate from FRED, quarterly; CBO’s natural rate of unemployment; prime-age participation and employment–population ratio, monthly and seasonally adjusted.
Sample
Plotted
Each point is one quarter of annualised real GDP growth against the change in the unemployment rate. The line is the fitted historical relationship; the last four quarters are connected in time order.
Main caveat
Full specification and diagnostics ↗
Would change this A four-quarter mean residual above +0.3 pp, or prime-age participation falling more than 0.5 pp below its February 2020 level.
02 Across workers

The weakness is concentrated: young graduates carry more unemployment than their own pre-2020 norm predicts.

Is the weakness spread evenly across workers, or is one group absorbing it?

How to read this section

Every group of workers has its own settled relationship to the national unemployment rate. When the economy weakens, unemployment rises faster for the young than for the old, and faster for workers without degrees than for those with them. Those ratios are stable enough to be useful: tell us the national rate and we can say what a given group’s rate ought to be.

So that is what we do. For each combination of age and education we learn that relationship from the fifteen years before the pandemic, then ask what the group’s unemployment rate should be today, given where the national rate actually is. All three charts below plot the same thing: the gap between that prediction and reality. Zero means a group is exactly where its own history says it should be. Positive means it is doing worse than its own track record predicts.

One extra step matters, because it changes the numbers. We tested whether the method returns zero when it should, by hiding the recent past and asking it to predict years we already know were unremarkable. It came back positive, by roughly half a point, so the procedure runs hot. That amount is subtracted from every figure on this page. What is left is the part the method cannot explain away as its own habit.

What each group has, against what the national rate predicts

What this chart does. It puts the two unemployment rates side by side for six groups. The hollow dot is the rate predicted from the national figure; the filled dot is the rate the group actually has. The bar between them is the gap. Read the lengths of the bars rather than their positions: one is conspicuously longer than the rest.

The same gap, across the whole age range

What this chart does. It takes the gap from the first chart and traces it across every five-year age band from the early twenties to the mid-sixties, so you can see where in the age range it sits rather than just that it exists. The grey band is the room the method’s own bias creates: a line inside it is not evidence of anything. Dot size is sample size, which is why the youngest graduate points are drawn smallest.

When the gap opened up

What this chart does. It answers the question the first two cannot: whether this is new. It follows the gap for young graduates month by month back to 2005. The grey band is the entire range this measure occupied from 2005 through 2019, the Great Recession included, so anything above the band is territory the pre-pandemic era never reached, in good years or bad.

The shape is the finding, and it is narrower than a story about young workers. Non-graduates in their twenties sit at essentially zero, and so do graduates past forty-five. What separates the affected group from the unaffected ones is not age alone and not education alone, but the combination: people at the start of a career that a degree was supposed to open.

The timing matters as much as the shape. This gap did not appear with the pandemic and then linger. It closed to almost nothing by early 2023 and has widened in most months since, which is the opposite of what a fading shock looks like.

What this cannot establish

Concentration, not cause. The same pattern would appear if firms had cut graduate training programs for ordinary cost reasons, or if degree supply had outrun demand in particular fields. The most serious alternative is compositional: as the share of young people finishing degrees rises, the average graduate is drawn from further down the distribution, which lifts the group’s unemployment rate relative to the national rate with no change in employer behaviour at all. Nothing here separates that from a demand story. The entry-level market was also weakening before generative AI was deployed at scale. Postings data by occupational exposure is what would distinguish these, and it is not in this tracker yet.

The technical specification
Data
IPUMS CPS basic monthly, , persons 16+, weighted by WTFINL. Unemployed is EMPSTAT ∈ {20,21,22}; the labor force is LABFORCE == 2. College+ is EDUC ≥ 111; HS+ (no BA) is 73 ≤ EDUC < 111.
Estimator
For each band g, ordinary least squares on months through :
log( rg,t ) = αg + βg · log( Rt ) + εg,t
where rg,t is the band’s trailing 12-month mean unemployment rate and Rt the same for all workers 16+. The fitted value is back-transformed as exp(·), so it targets the conditional median rather than the mean. β is a cyclical elasticity: below one means the band is less cycle-sensitive than the aggregate.
Statistic
The mean of (actual − predicted) over the latest months, in rate units, then less the placebo bias below. Because the fit is multiplicative, a gap in percentage points scales with the band’s base rate, so the actual-to-predicted ratio is the like-for-like comparison across groups; both are in the tooltips.
Bands
Five single years of age wide, plotted at the centre. The lower edge of the youngest band is pinned at 21 for College+ and 18 for HS+ (no BA), so no band spans an age at which the credential is effectively unattainable. < HS is excluded: below 21 that category is defined by an outcome that is mechanically age-dependent, and its share of the young population more than halved over the sample, so its residuals track who remains in the category rather than labor demand.
Placebo correction
The same procedure re-run with the training cut moved back, then evaluated over the two following years, which were ordinary:
    Mean error is almost identical to mean absolute error in the original diagnostics, so the miss is one-directional across nearly every band: bias, not noise. The mechanism is that the aggregate rate is not a sufficient statistic for a group’s rate, because band-level β drifts as educational composition shifts, so a falling aggregate makes the fit over-predict improvement. The correction is estimated per band and subtracted. It matters most for comparisons between groups, since HS+ carries the larger bias.
    Moving average
    Taken over 12 calendar months, requiring at least 11 observed. October 2025 CPS was never collected, so a positional 12-row average would have silently spanned 13 calendar months for every window in the current reporting period.
    Diagnostics
    Known limits
    No standard errors are placed on the gap itself; the placebo band is what stands in for them, and it is estimated from two scenarios only, so the headline is better read as a range than a point. The youngest graduate cells are thin. Each point is a 12-month average and the window closes in , so this is a slow-moving object describing roughly the year to then, not a current-month reading.
    Full specification and diagnostics ↗
    Would change this The bias-adjusted young-graduate gap falling back inside its pre-2020 range, a matched postings series showing the same pattern in occupations with no plausible AI exposure, or degree-attainment shares accounting for the drift.
    03 Across industries

    The industries using AI most have added jobs fastest: the high-adoption third stands at against for the low-adoption third, on 2019 = 100.

    If AI displaces workers, the industries buying it should be the ones shedding jobs. Are they?

    How to read sections 03 and 04

    The Census Business Trends and Outlook Survey asks roughly a million businesses, every two weeks, whether they used AI to produce goods or services. Averaging each industry’s answers gives one number per industry: the share of its firms using AI. Sort industries by that number, cut them into three equal groups, and you have the high, middle and low adoption groups plotted below.

    Then ignore the survey entirely and watch what BLS reports for those groups. Every line in these two sections is payroll or turnover data. Adoption is used only to decide which industries go in which group, which is what makes this a descriptive cut rather than an estimate of anything.

    Two features of the measure matter throughout. It counts firms, not workers, and adopters skew large, so the share of employees inside an AI-using firm runs well above these figures. And the survey rewrote the question in November 2025, so the grouping uses only the earlier, consistent wording.

    Employment by AI-adoption group, indexed to 2019

    What this chart does. It stacks the three groups on a common base, so the vertical distance between lines is the difference in growth since 2019, not in size. The displacement hypothesis predicts the high-adoption line ends up lowest. It ends up highest, and has done throughout.

    Which sectors are in each group

    This is the cut most likely to be screenshotted, in either direction, so it is worth being clear about what it is not. It is not evidence that AI creates jobs. The ordering here is mostly a statement about which industries were growing before anyone typed a prompt, and about which ones the pandemic knocked down hardest.

    What it does establish is a floor for the argument. Any claim that AI is visibly subtracting jobs at the industry level has to explain why the industries doing the adopting are the ones that grew fastest, and it has to do that with something more than the raw series.

    What this cannot establish

    Almost nothing, on its own. The gap that opens in 2020–22 is pandemic composition rather than AI: the low-adoption group is accommodation and food services, construction and transportation, which fell hardest in 2020 and were still climbing back into 2024. Adoption is also not randomly assigned, and the causation plausibly runs backwards, since profitable growing firms have the slack to buy new technology. Eighteen sectors is a coarse grid, and BTOS counts firms while CES counts jobs, so the two sides of this comparison are weighted differently.

    The technical specification
    Treatment
    Each sector’s mean BTOS “currently using AI” share, firm-weighted, over collection periods before the survey rewrote the question. Sectors are cut at the terciles of that distribution, six per group.
    Outcome
    BLS Current Employment Statistics, all employees, seasonally adjusted. Employment is summed within each group and indexed to the group’s own 2019 mean, so the lines carry growth rather than level.
    Sample
    Known limits
    Firm-weighted treatment against a worker-weighted outcome. No controls of any kind: not for pre-trend, not for pandemic catch-up, not for industry composition. With eighteen sectors there is no power to detect a modest effect, so the absence of a negative gradient here is weak evidence of absence rather than strong evidence of nothing.
    Would change this The high-adoption index falling below the low-adoption index, or the gap narrowing once each sector’s 2017–19 trend and its distance from the 2019 level are conditioned out.
    04 Hiring and firing

    Mostly a freeze rather than a purge. Hires and quits are below their 2019 levels in every group and furthest below where adoption is highest — but that group is also the only one whose layoffs rate, at , is back above where it started.

    A payroll count nets hiring against separations. Which side of that is moving, and does it move differently where AI is used?

    Openings, hires, quits and layoffs by AI-adoption group
    JOLTS rates, three-month moving average, employment-weighted within each group

    What this chart does. It separates the two things a payroll number adds together. Openings and hires are demand for new workers; quits are workers’ own confidence; layoffs are firms shedding staff. Displacement by automation has a signature: hiring falls, layoffs stay flat, and the gap opens where the technology is used. Read the levels against the 2019 stretch on the left of each panel, and read the distance between the lines within each panel.

    Which supersectors are in each group

    Most of that is the low-hire, low-fire economy everyone has been describing, and it is not specific to AI: the three groups turn together, and openings have round-tripped to roughly where they were in 2019 across all of them. The exception is the last panel. Layoffs are the one series where the ordering runs the way a displacement story predicts, and the high-adoption group is the only one that has not returned to its 2019 rate.

    What this cannot establish

    Read the layoffs panel with its composition in mind. The largest employer in the high-adoption group is professional and business services, which JOLTS reports as one supersector pooling NAICS 54, 55 and 56 — and 56 contains temporary help services, the most volatile employment in the survey and a sector that has been shedding jobs since 2022 for reasons that long predate generative AI. A tenth of a percentage point spread across five supersectors is not a finding that can be pinned on anything.

    More generally: fifteen supersectors, five per group, is the coarsest grid on this page, and these units are broader than the CES sectors in section 03. A displacement effect concentrated in one occupation inside one of them would be invisible. These are also rates, not counts, so a group whose employment base is growing can post a falling hires rate while hiring more people — which, given section 03, is exactly what the high-adoption group has been doing.

    The technical specification
    Treatment
    The same pre-break BTOS adoption measure as section 03, mapped from BTOS sectors to JOLTS supersectors by analysis/src/lookups/crosswalk_btos_jolts.csv, then cut at terciles, five supersectors per group.
    Outcome
    BLS Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey, seasonally adjusted rates. Within a group, rates are averaged across supersectors weighted by employment, then smoothed with a three-month trailing mean.
    Sample
    Scale
    Each panel is free-scaled, so vertical distances are not comparable between panels. The layoffs panel is clipped: its three-month average peaks near ten percent in spring 2020, and at full scale the entire post-2021 range would be a few pixels tall. The clip level, the true peaks and the exit points are all marked; the figures are in the chart note.
    Known limits
    Same firm-weighted-treatment problem as section 03. Openings are a percent of employment plus openings and so are not on the same denominator as the other three. Nothing here is conditioned on anything.
    Would change this The high-adoption layoffs gap surviving the removal of professional and business services from that group, which would rule out temporary help as the explanation. Or the gap widening beyond a few tenths of a point, which is where it stops being noise across five supersectors.
    05 Early careers

    One test does find something: early-career hiring is weaker per standard deviation of industry adoption. Then the timing undoes most of the AI reading of it.

    Sections 03 and 04 compare industries in aggregate. What happens with a sharper instrument, one that compares young and prime-age workers inside the same industry?

    How to read this section

    The problem with every comparison above is that industries differ for a hundred reasons besides AI. This test removes all of them at once. For each industry it takes the change in hiring of 22 to 24 year olds and subtracts the change in hiring of 35 to 44 year olds in that same industry. Anything that hit the whole industry, a demand collapse or a post-pandemic correction, drops out of the difference.

    What is left is whether young workers specifically did worse in the industries that adopted AI. The data is the Census LEHD Quarterly Workforce Indicators, which counts actual hires by age from state unemployment insurance records rather than from a survey.

    Change in hiring, 22–24 minus 35–44, against adoption

    What this chart does. Each dot is a subsector. Moving right means more AI adoption; moving down means early-career hiring fell further than prime-age hiring in that same industry. The line slopes down, and it is the most precisely estimated relationship on this page.

    That result compares two windows, 2019 against the most recent four quarters. It cannot say when the gap opened, and a two-window comparison cannot tell a gap that opened the month ChatGPT shipped from one that opened in April 2020 and never closed. So run the same regression once per quarter against the same 2019 base.

    The same coefficient, estimated every quarter

    What this chart does. It replaces one number with its history. Flat through 2019 is the pre-trend, and it is the part that supports the design. Then watch where the drop happens relative to the purple line.

    So the cross-section is real and the AI reading of it is much narrower than it looks. The gap between young and prime-age hiring in high-adoption industries is a pandemic artifact that never closed, with a further leg since 2023 that is consistent with AI diffusion and equally consistent with the tech correction, elevated interest rates, or the same industries simply continuing what they started in 2020.

    What this cannot establish

    Adoption is measured at the industry level and outcomes at the industry level, so this is not the firm-level test the displacement literature actually needs. No public source links firm-level AI adoption to worker-level outcomes. The strongest objection to the cross-section survives the age difference: industries that adopted AI early are more white-collar, more urban, and were more exposed to the post-2021 tech correction, and the age difference removes what hit those industries uniformly, not something that hit their young workers specifically.

    The technical specification
    Data
    LEHD Quarterly Workforce Indicators, all private ownership, hires and employment by NAICS subsector and age band, joined to pre-break BTOS adoption at the subsector level. Young is QWI age band A03 (22–24), prime-age is A05 (35–44). Hires are trailing four-quarter sums, which removes seasonality without an adjustment model.
    Estimator
    Cross-sectional OLS across subsectors of the age-differenced change in log hires on standardised adoption:
    Δlog Hi,22-24 − Δlog Hi,35-44 = α + β · z(adoptioni) + εi
    The event study is this same regression re-estimated once per quarter against a fixed 2019 base. At the final quarter it reproduces the cross-section, and the build asserts that equality.
    All specifications
    Power
    Status
    Known limits
    Industry-level treatment, industry-level outcome. No standard errors are clustered beyond the cross-section, and with 59 subsectors the leverage of any single one is non-trivial. Coverage of the QWI panel is incomplete in the most recent quarters, so the last point moves as states report.
    Would change this The quarterly coefficient continuing to fall through 2026 while the pandemic leg stays flat, which would put the weight of the effect in the AI era rather than in 2020. Or firm-level evidence, which would replace this test rather than adjust it.
    Taken together

    This is a tracker, not a verdict. Readings are regenerated when the underlying data refreshes, each section states the threshold that would move it, and further tests are added as they are built. The methods page carries the estimating equations, samples and known failure modes.

    About

    Purpose

    This tracker is a curated research intelligence tool at the intersection of artificial intelligence, automation, and labor markets. It aggregates peer-reviewed studies, policy reports, and investigative journalism into a structured database — and synthesizes that research into strategic themes and policy frameworks — to support institutional positioning, workforce strategy, and policy analysis.

    Created by

    Christelle Prophete. This site is independently maintained and updated as new research emerges. The content does not reflect the opinions or perspectives of the creator.

    Papers tab

    A filterable card database of individual research entries, tagged by category and geographic scope. Cards can be filtered by category and geography, or searched by title, source, or finding.

    Themes (archived)

    Cross-cutting syntheses of the research database. Each theme frames a key strategic question, presents an evidence consensus, identifies implications for institutional actors, and notes gaps in the current evidence base. This view has been retired from the main site and is preserved at prototypes/themes.html.

    Policy Map tab

    Twenty-seven policy interventions organized by category and mapped to five stages of AI-driven labor disruption — from Repair (fixes needed regardless of AI's trajectory) through Transform (responses to large-scale displacement of the workforce). Each policy card includes a plain-language description, an account of the implementation challenge, and links to supporting research in the database. Does not constitute policy advice.

    AI Disclaimer

    Summaries, key findings, and takeaways are AI-generated and reviewed for accuracy on an ongoing basis. They are intended as orientation aids — not substitutes for reading the original source. Always consult the primary publication before citing or acting on any finding.
